name: Chiropractic neck adjustment

lead: A chiropractic neck adjustment is a thrust applied to the joints of the cervical spine, usually by a chiropractor. In appearance communities it is sought for better head and neck posture, and occasionally for jaw or face alignment, aiming for a more balanced profile.

A quick, small-amplitude thrust is applied to a cervical joint, often producing a popping sound, and practitioners say it restores joint movement. Research on cervical manipulation concerns neck pain: a 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence, while a smaller body of moderate-to-low-quality evidence suggests multiple sessions may improve pain and function compared with some medications. No study evaluates it for facial appearance.

paras: People book sessions with a chiropractor, often a series, sometimes alongside posture exercises. A session takes minutes and the thrust is felt immediately.

The main concern is vertebral artery dissection, which can lead to stroke; case reports also describe cerebellar infarction and preretinal hemorrhages after neck manipulation. A 2001 study reported higher rates of vertebrobasilar stroke in adults under 45 who had recently visited a chiropractor, with no significant association over 45, and some chiropractors dispute a causal link.

angle.text: Some appearance communities seek neck adjustments to improve head and neck posture and alignment, hoping for a more balanced profile. Manipulation has been studied for neck pain, and an appearance effect has not been tested.

lead: A chiropractic neck adjustment, or cervical spinal manipulation, is a quick, small-amplitude thrust applied to the joints of the neck, usually by a chiropractor, osteopath or physiotherapist. Practitioners use it for neck pain, stiffness and cervicogenic headache, and some people in appearance communities seek it out in the hope of improving head and neck posture, which they associate with a straighter profile, a tidier jawline and a better-aligned look.

The posture-to-looks chain is a claimed one: proponents describe freer neck movement as supporting better head position, and head position is widely discussed as influencing how the jaw, chin and neck read in profile. No study has tested neck manipulation for facial appearance. The published research concerns pain and function. A 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence for spinal manipulation in neck pain, while some lower-quality evidence suggests multiple sessions may improve pain and function compared with some medications [1].
Safety is the most discussed topic in the literature. Vertebral artery dissection and stroke are the main reported serious harms, and reviewers say their frequency is uncertain [1][2][3].

paras: Cervical manipulation is usually a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, often accompanied by an audible pop. It is widely used by physiotherapists, chiropractors, osteopaths and doctors for neck pain and cervicogenic headache [4]. A related literature tests manipulation of the upper cervical spine in people with temporomandibular disorder, a jaw pain condition, usually combined with other treatments [5].

Spinal manipulation, which chiropractors call a spinal adjustment, is the most common treatment in chiropractic care. Wikipedia describes it as a passive manoeuvre that takes a joint complex past its usual range of movement without dislocating it, defined by a dynamic thrust that often produces an audible release.[6] Chiropractic began in the late nineteenth century with founder D. D. Palmer, whose idea of vertebral subluxation as a disturbance to the body's innate healing ability remains a point of difference between chiropractors who follow that philosophy and the many who limit their work to musculoskeletal complaints.[6]

Wikipedia's chiropractic article reports that most people seek care for low back pain, that neck and back pain are the field's main focus, and that research on effectiveness has been of mixed quality, with studies by chiropractors tending to reach more favourable conclusions than reviews by outside authors.[6] The same article reports that the World Health Organization found chiropractic care in general safe when used skilfully and appropriately, while noting that data are not sufficient to establish the safety of manipulation.[6]

A 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence for spinal manipulation in neck pain, and a 2007 review reported moderate-to-high-quality evidence of benefit for chronic neck pain not caused by whiplash [1]. A multicentre randomised trial in 120 people with temporomandibular disorder compared dry needling plus upper cervical manipulation with splint therapy, diclofenac and joint mobilisation [5]. Effects on facial or postural appearance have not been studied.

Reviewers describe little evidence of harm and little evidence of safety, and note that under-reporting is likely substantial [1]. A 2001 Stroke study found vertebrobasilar accidents were five times more likely in adults under 45 who had visited a chiropractor in the preceding week, with no significant association above 45; some chiropractors dispute that manipulation causes these events [1].

A 2013 systematic review of case reports found 43 articles describing 901 cervical artery dissections and 707 strokes reported in association with manipulation, and assessed the quality of those reports [2]. A 2017 systematic review of 144 studies covering 227 adverse-event cases found that cervical artery dissection was reported in 57 percent of them and that screening tests for at-risk patients appear unreliable [7]. A 2024 meta-analysis of randomised trials notes that the link between manipulation and serious events rests mostly on case-control studies and case reports, which cannot establish incidence or causation [4].

Individual case reports describe cerebellar infarction after a chiropractor's neck manipulation [8], preretinal haemorrhages after high-velocity cervical manipulation [9], and a fatal vertebral artery dissection in a woman who performed manipulation on herself [3].

Wikipedia's chiropractic article reports estimates of serious events following neck manipulation that range from about 5 strokes per 100,000 manipulations to 1.46 serious adverse events per 10 million manipulations, and states that the data were inadequate to be conclusive.[6] It also reports that vertebrobasilar stroke is statistically associated with chiropractic visits in people under 45 but is similarly associated with visits to a general practitioner, which some researchers interpret as pointing to existing symptoms of a dissection that prompt both kinds of visit.[6] Mild, brief effects such as soreness or headache are reported far more often, in an estimated 33 to 61 percent of patients, and usually fade within one to two days.[6]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of biomechanical studies found that the strain placed on the vertebral artery during cervical manipulation was lower than during passive range-of-motion movements at the upper levels measured.[10]

sections.h: Use in lifting and looksmaxxing communities
paras: Chiropractic visits come up in strength-training forums as part of managing neck and upper-back tightness rather than as a facial-aesthetics tool. One T Nation user wrote of a first chiropractor visit that he now understood why the lifter-influencer David Laid recommends it, describing heat, cold, clicking and acupuncture.[11] Another lifter reported that a visit really helped his neck and traps.[12]

The appearance chain people describe runs through posture: a neck that moves freely holds the head more upright, which can change how the jaw and neck read in profile. Reviews of spinal manipulation address pain and function, and no study has measured facial or profile change after a neck adjustment.[1][6]

No studies found on neck adjustment for facial appearance. Trials of cervical manipulation address neck pain, jaw disorders and short-term physiological measures, and the safety literature consists largely of case reports and reviews [1][4][5][8][9].

A 2025 biomechanics review pooled six studies of vertebral artery strain and found lower strain during manipulation than during passive rotation at the upper cervical segments.[10] A randomised multicentre trial in 120 people with temporomandibular disorder compared dry needling with upper cervical manipulation against splint therapy, diclofenac and joint mobilisation.[5]

lore.intro: Chiropractic neck work appears in lifting and appearance circles mostly as a way to relieve tightness and keep the neck moving, with occasional talk of posture and neck-line benefits.[11][12]
